    The reflection functor is fully faithful where the incoming sum is onto #

    The Bernstein-Gelfand-Ponomarev reflection C⁺ᵢ at a sink i replaces the vertex space Mᵢ by the kernel of the sum LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.incomingSum of the arrows into i. It annihilates the vertex simple Sᵢ, so it cannot be an equivalence; what it is, is fully faithful on the representations whose incoming sum at i is onto. This file proves that: whenever the sum of the arrows into i is onto for M, the map (M ⟶ N) → (C⁺ᵢ M ⟶ C⁺ᵢ N) supplied by LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor is a bijection. Only the source M needs the hypothesis; the target N is arbitrary.

    Surjectivity of the incoming sum is the hypothesis throughout; it is not equivalent to avoiding Sᵢ. It is LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.incomingSum_surjective_of_indecomposable that ties the two together, and only for an indecomposable M: such an M has its incoming sum at i onto as soon as it is not isomorphic to Sᵢ. So the vertex simple names the exceptional case only among indecomposables, and that is the only place below where it is mentioned.

    Both halves are elementary once the incoming sum is available. Faithfulness is the surjectivity of that sum: a morphism reflecting to zero has vanishing components away from i, hence, by LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.incomingSum_naturality, its component at i kills the range of the incoming sum, which is everything. Fullness is the first isomorphism theorem: a morphism θ of the reflected representations carries the kernel at i for M into the kernel for N, so the composite ⨁_{a : b ⟶ i} M_b → ⨁_{a : b ⟶ i} N_b → Nᵢ factors through the incoming sum of M, and the resulting map Mᵢ → Nᵢ completes the components of θ away from i to a morphism M ⟶ N reflecting back to θ.

    The consequence is that reflection at a sink preserves indecomposability. The reflection functor is additive, so a bijection on endomorphisms matches idempotents with idempotents; an indecomposable M other than Sᵢ therefore reflects to an indecomposable representation of the reflected quiver. No finite-dimensionality is needed for that. It is needed for the other half of the induction step: LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.dimVector_reflectRep_of_indecomposable computes the dimension vector of the reflection as sᵢ · dim M when the vertex spaces at the sources of the arrows into i are finite-dimensional.

    Main results #

    • LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_injective, LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_surjective and LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_bijective: the reflection functor at a sink is fully faithful on the representations whose incoming sum there is onto.
    • LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.nonempty_iso_of_nonempty_iso_reflectRep: the reflection functor at a sink reflects isomorphisms between representations whose incoming sums there are onto.
    • LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.indecomposable_reflectRep: reflection at a sink preserves indecomposability, under the same hypothesis.
    • LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.indecomposable_reflectRep_of_not_nonempty_iso_simpleRep: the same statement with the hypothesis discharged, for an indecomposable representation other than the vertex simple Sᵢ.

    Implementation notes #

    The reflection functor's object (reflectionFunctor i hi).obj M is only propositionally equal to LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectRep M hi, because the body of the functor is not exposed outside the module defining it. The statements below therefore speak of the functor's map, whose type mentions only the functor, and the vertex spaces of its objects are named by the two private transports reflectObj_self and reflectObj_of_ne, which are exactly the composites appearing in LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_app_self_apply and LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_app_of_ne. Proof irrelevance makes them interchangeable with the transports written inline there.

    As in the neighbouring files, a vertex i : Q is used both as an object of CategoryTheory.Paths and as a vertex of LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.Quiver.Reflect Q i, identifications that hold only by unfolding semireducible definitions. Goals mentioning both are therefore not type-correct at the transparency rw and simp build motives with, so every step that strips a conjugation by eqToHom is factored through the general transport lemmas in LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.Categorical.EqToHom, which subst the object equalities away before doing anything.

    The linear section of the incoming sum used to build the preimage exists because a vector space is projective; the private sinkSection is a choice of one. Nothing downstream depends on which section is chosen: the private homSink_incomingSum pins the resulting map on the whole of Mᵢ, and it is the only property of that map the proofs use.

    References #

    See Bernstein--Gelfand--Ponomarev, Coxeter functors and Gabriel's theorem, and Derksen--Weyman, An Introduction to Quiver Representations, Ch. 2.

    Faithfulness #

    source
    theorem LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_injective {k : Type u} {Q : Type v} [Field k] [Quiver Q] [Fintype Q] [(a b : Q) → Fintype (a ⟶ b)] {M N : QuiverRep k Q} {i : Q} (hi : Quiver.IsSink i) (hs : Function.Surjective ⇑(incomingSum M i)) :
    Function.Injective fun (η : M ⟶ N) => (reflectionFunctor i hi).map η

    The reflection functor at a sink is faithful on the representations whose incoming sum there is onto. Two morphisms with the same reflection agree away from the sink, because reflection leaves those components alone; at the sink they then agree on the range of the incoming sum, by LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.incomingSum_naturality, and that range is everything.

    Fullness #

    A morphism θ of reflected representations is taken apart into its components away from the sink and the map it induces between the two kernels there, and those pieces are reassembled into a morphism of the original representations.

    Full faithfulness, and indecomposability #

    theorem LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_surjective {k : Type u} {Q : Type v} [Field k] [Quiver Q] [Fintype Q] [(a b : Q) → Fintype (a ⟶ b)] {M N : QuiverRep k Q} {i : Q} (hi : Quiver.IsSink i) (hs : Function.Surjective ⇑(incomingSum M i)) :
    Function.Surjective fun (η : M ⟶ N) => (reflectionFunctor i hi).map η

    The reflection functor at a sink is full on the representations whose incoming sum there is onto.

    source
    theorem LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_bijective {k : Type u} {Q : Type v} [Field k] [Quiver Q] [Fintype Q] [(a b : Q) → Fintype (a ⟶ b)] {M N : QuiverRep k Q} {i : Q} (hi : Quiver.IsSink i) (hs : Function.Surjective ⇑(incomingSum M i)) :
    Function.Bijective fun (η : M ⟶ N) => (reflectionFunctor i hi).map η

    The reflection functor at a sink is fully faithful on the representations whose incoming sum there is onto, a class that by LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.incomingSum_surjective_of_indecomposable contains every indecomposable representation other than the vertex simple Sᵢ.

    source
    theorem LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.nonempty_iso_of_nonempty_iso_reflectRep {k : Type u} {Q : Type v} [Field k] [Quiver Q] [Fintype Q] [(a b : Q) → Fintype (a ⟶ b)] {M N : QuiverRep k Q} {i : Q} (hi : Quiver.IsSink i) (hsM : Function.Surjective ⇑(incomingSum M i)) (hsN : Function.Surjective ⇑(incomingSum N i)) (h : Nonempty (reflectRep M hi ≅ reflectRep N hi)) :
    Nonempty (M ≅ N)

    The reflection functor at a sink reflects isomorphisms, between representations whose incoming sums there are onto. Fullness produces morphisms f : M ⟶ N and g : N ⟶ M reflecting to the two halves of the given isomorphism, and faithfulness turns the two triangle identities downstairs into the two upstairs.

    The reflection functor is not fully faithful on all of LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.QuiverRep k Q -- it annihilates the vertex simple at i -- so CategoryTheory.Functor.ReflectsIsomorphisms and the machinery around it, which ask for Full and Faithful instances, do not apply, and the argument is made directly from LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_surjective and LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.reflectionFunctor_map_injective.

    source
    theorem LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.indecomposable_reflectRep {k : Type u} {Q : Type v} [Field k] [Quiver Q] [Fintype Q] [(a b : Q) → Fintype (a ⟶ b)] {M : QuiverRep k Q} {i : Q} (hi : Quiver.IsSink i) (hM : CategoryTheory.Indecomposable M) (hs : Function.Surjective ⇑(incomingSum M i)) :
    CategoryTheory.Indecomposable (reflectRep M hi)

    Reflection at a sink preserves indecomposability, as soon as the sum of the arrows into the sink is onto. Reflection is additive and bijective on the endomorphisms of M, so it matches the idempotents of M with those of its reflection; an indecomposable has only the trivial ones, and the reflection of the identity is the identity while the reflection of 0 is 0.

    The vertex simple as the exceptional case #

    As in LargeIndecomposable.Foundations.RepresentationTheory.Quiver.Reflection.Indecomposable, a statement naming both a reflected representation and the vertex simple has to put the quiver, its arrows and the field in one universe.
